title: How to Choose What to Read
text:
“Read this...”
“No.”
“Don’t criticize it until you’ve read it!”

Choosing what to read is a serious and important process. The world has too much written, said, and filmed for anyone to see it all. In one lifetime, you need to manage to encounter what matters most. So not everything people recommend is worth reading.

By what criteria should we choose? Everyone decides for themselves. There are several factors before the book is even in your hands:

1. Fame. It matters in a way: a good book becomes known over time.
2. Recognition. Classics and the like should come first.
3. Title. No, this is not “judging by the cover.” The title is part of the book, and an important one, because people judge by it.
4. Description. If you are deciding whether to read something, read the description. Spoilers...

title: Childhood Friends
text:
Childhood friends. Influence on the subconscious. Being raised by one another. Love from childhood.

Now, in plain language. Dmitry Sergeyevich Likhachev wrote in *Letters About the Good and the Beautiful* that childhood is a period of closeness, and therefore lifelong friends are made in deep childhood. But he did not explain why. I have a hypothesis.

Freud wrote that a person’s character is shaped mostly by childhood. Impressions received in childhood leave a mark for life and make a person who they are. So when two people come together in childhood, they strongly influence one another; they “raise” each other. One person’s character adapts to the unevenness of the other’s character, and vice versa. That is why, even as adults, they find it easier to be together: their characters fit.

This leads to a thought: the best partners would be people children had known since childhood. No irritating traits and so on. It is very easy for you with Lena, after all.

For some reason, though, children rarely socialize with children of the opposite sex in childhood. Most likely because of jokes from parents, teachers, and classmates.

Perhaps now I understand the Indian practice in which the family chooses whom a son will marry: his childhood friend. That may be why marriages are happy in many cases.

title: The Consensus State
text:
I am reading *And Quiet Flows the Don*. Do you know what I like about Bolshevik politics? They knew how to talk. Objectively, at the early stage most people were not on their side, but the “agitators” talked to people, won arguments, and drew them over. That was not dumb propaganda; it was honest heart-to-heart conversation.

In *Andromeda: A Space-Age Tale*, society is shown as one where power belongs not to the majority, as in our world, but to everyone. Decisions are made only unanimously. Society works for the happiness of each person, not the majority. No one is oppressed.

I used to wonder: is that even possible? Could not a single person object? I thought it was a utopia. Now I think there is probably always a solution. Two people, if they talk and think enough, can always reach a consensus, a solution convenient for both, if each thinks about the other and can understand the other’s position.

So imagine a form of government where every decision is accepted by nationwide confirmation, for example in a mobile app or on a website. If even one person is against it, a government representative comes to them or writes to ask why they disagree. They argue and reach a common solution. Maybe that person receives special rights if the issue comes from some personal circumstance. If that person wins the argument, the law might even be passed in the opposite direction. This would produce a state where every person supports government decisions, without the state becoming rigid or inert.

text:
Army versus science.

I concluded that in the modern world it is not as important to make a product quickly as it is to make it well. Therefore a subordinate can say to a manager, “I think you are mistaken here and here.” The manager will consider it and make a better decision.

Still, this idea can be used when something truly needs to be done quickly. For example, at hackathons: agree that the team lead’s orders are not discussed. Time is very limited—two days.

title: Markets and Predictable Fluctuations
text:
Remember how you said that on a universal exchange the price of flour would rise in winter and fall in summer?

Remember how dad said that bonds rise before a payout?

This is exactly the invisible hand of the market. Suppose that was true for a while. Then smart people would start buying and selling, profiting from that jump again and again. Their turnover would grow until the jump balanced out. So in an ideal market there are no fluctuations at all—only unpredictable ones.

title: The Evolution of Cultures
text:
Toward thoughts about the evolution of cultures. Cultures do not die by themselves. They are displaced by stronger ones. When the strongest appears, the others either adapt or die. For example, a people ready to work twelve hours a day will force other peoples to work the same amount.

The Greeks would not have wanted to build up their army if not for the Spartans.

One could try to invent the currently ideal culture. People live underground in bunkers: there is no point in building missile defense against them — shoot as much as you want, you will not reach them. Culture and entertainment are banned: only study and work. For reproduction, take an example from a fictional system: 100% birth control.

The question of public dissatisfaction arises. Total control? For now, let us not think about the transition to this order. The task is only to formulate it.

Another example: China increasing GDP while neglecting spending on entertainment. Others will have to do the same or lose.

And the method of transition is very simple: raising children as in a fictional society. Different religions for different personality types? A camera embedded in the forehead and a GPS tag.

Addition after reading The Selfish Gene: one must account for the fact that not all cultures are ESS. That is, when dissatisfaction with life becomes too high, culture obviously changes.

title: The Selfish Gene and Cultural Evolution
text:
About Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene. He shows that some species have an altruism gene that determines their behavior, while others do not. A person reading this subconsciously applies the same scheme to humans. It seems to them that people can likewise help one another or refuse to help.

That is the point of the book: to understand how nature determines our desire to help others. But this is exactly where a contradiction appears. A person is determined less by nature, that is, by genes, and more by mentality — by the culture imposed on them. Even if genes say “steal and kill,” a person can still refuse to do it simply because they were raised that way.

That is the first thought. The next thought: on the other hand, history contains the same evolution of cultures. Just as genes evolve on the biological level, culture evolves too. This means that Richard Dawkins’s reasoning about altruistic genes and other animals applies to culture as well. From this point of view, it is very interesting.

title: Everyone Has Their Own Catastrophe
text:
An AI psychologist gently flicks you on the forehead: “Because everyone has their own personal catastrophe, and you are not part of it.”

The myth: “Everyone is looking, judging, whispering.”

Reality: most people are wearing headphones and scrolling TikTok, some are nervously preparing for their own presentation, and some do not even remember your name.

Why do they not care?

They do not have your dossier. To them, you are a background character. They do not know your social media, your grades, or your private worries.

They are scared too. Everyone is worried about their appearance, their coursework, and their awkward moments.

The human brain is selfish: it spends most of its energy on itself. At most, you are “oh, a couple,” and then forgotten.

How can you check this? Tomorrow, try to remember what the most noticeable person in the group wore yesterday. You do not remember? They do not remember you either.

Even if two people notice and judge, that is two out of a hundred in the hallway. Is their opinion worth your happiness?

Reverse the scenario: if you see another couple, do you laugh, remember them for a year, or think about your lab work five minutes later?

The world does not revolve around you, and that is liberating. You are free to be with the person dear to you.

And if someone does glance over, just hold your beloved person’s hand tighter. Let them envy you.
